title: Chemistry 11 — Chapter 7: The Ammonia Batch
description: Friday's ammonia synthesis run needs a full stoichiometry workup — mole ratios, mass calculations, which reactant actually runs out first, and how much of the batch was actually recovered.

mika.name: Ms. Mika Tan
mika.description: Has run this reaction a thousand times and can smell a bad ratio.

dev.name: Dev
dev.description: Thinks more reactant always means more product.

periodic_table.name: Periodic Table Card
periodic_table.description: Molar masses for every element, right where you need them.

reaction_sheet.name: Reaction Sheet
reaction_sheet.description: The balanced equation and available reactant quantities for Friday's batch.

elements.text: Friday's ammonia batch needs a full workup — mole ratios, mass, which reactant runs out first, and the actual yield once it's done.
Can't we just throw in extra of everything so nothing runs short?

elements.prompt: Mika hands you the reaction sheet.

options.text: "No — the mole ratios tell us exactly what we need, and exactly what'll be left over."

elements.text: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, balanced. Those coefficients are a mole ratio: 1 mole of nitrogen always reacts with exactly 3 moles of hydrogen to produce 2 moles of ammonia — no more, no less.

config.question: For the unbalanced equation N2 + H2 -> NH3, what are the correct coefficients?
config.explanation: Balancing nitrogen and hydrogen atoms on both sides requires N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3.

config.prompt: Using N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, how many moles of H2 are needed to react completely with 2.0 mol of N2?

elements.text: Going from grams to grams always follows the same chain: balance the equation, convert given mass to moles, apply the mole ratio, then convert the answer back to grams.

config.prompt: Order these steps of a stoichiometry calculation from first to last.

items.text: Apply the mole ratio from the equation
Convert answer moles back to grams

config.prompt: Ammonia's molar mass is 17.0 g/mol. Starting from 2.0 mol N2 (which produces 4.0 mol NH3 via the 1:2 ratio), how many grams of NH3 form?

elements.text: Today's batch only has 3.0 mol of H2 on hand, not 6.0. Does that break the calculation?

It changes it — that's the limiting reagent. With 2.0 mol N2, you'd need 6.0 mol H2 to react all of it, but only 3.0 mol H2 is available. Whichever reactant runs out first caps how much product can form, no matter how much of the other one is sitting around.

config.question: 2.0 mol N2 and 3.0 mol H2 are available. Fully reacting the N2 would require 6.0 mol H2, but only 3.0 mol H2 is on hand. Which reactant is limiting?

options.text: H2 — it runs out before all the N2 can react
N2 — there's less of it in absolute moles
Both run out at exactly the same time
Neither — there's always enough of both

config.explanation: The reactant that runs out first, based on the mole ratio the equation actually requires, is the limiting reagent — here that's H2, not whichever has fewer moles in isolation.

config.prompt: Using H2 as the limiting reagent (3.0 mol available, ratio 3 mol H2 -> 2 mol NH3), how many moles of NH3 can actually form?

elements.text: Theoretical yield is what the math predicts under perfect conditions — 2.0 mol NH3 here. Real reactions rarely hit that exactly, so percent yield compares what you actually collected to what the theory predicted: (actual / theoretical) x 100.

config.prompt: Theoretical yield was 2.0 mol NH3; the batch actually recovered 1.5 mol. What is the percent yield, to 1 decimal place, no % sign?

config.question: A percent yield of exactly 100% would mean:

options.text: The full theoretical amount, based on the limiting reagent, was actually collected
The reaction used no limiting reagent at all
Twice as much product formed as the calculation predicted
The reaction produced no measurable product

config.explanation: 100% yield means the actual amount recovered exactly matched the theoretical maximum the limiting reagent allowed.

elements.text: Ratios, mass, limiting reagent, and yield — the full workup checks out. Friday's batch is documented correctly.
We got through it, but a step or two was shaky. Let's revisit the limiting reagent logic before the next batch.

elements.prompt: The order form is submitted. What now?

options.text: Show Dev why 'more reactant' doesn't help once the other one runs out.
Sign off. The batch is documented — that's enough for today.

elements.text: So the coefficients set the ratio, the limiting reagent caps how much can actually form, and yield just tells you how close reality got to that cap. It's one chain, not four separate topics.

ending.title: Stoichiometry Hero
ending.description: Worked the full stoichiometry chain from mole ratios through percent yield, and corrected Dev's 'more reactant' assumption.

ending.title: Batch Documented
ending.description: The workup is complete and the batch is documented. The deeper limiting-reagent lesson can wait.
